svg.aria-label: Storage layout of the Orin Nano Developer Kit. Left: the 64 MiB QSPI-NOR flash on the module holds the boot configuration table and two complete boot chains, A and B, each with MB1, MB2, UEFI, the secure OS and the firmware of the other processors. Right: the root device (SD card, NVMe SSD or USB drive) holds a GPT with kernel and kernel-dtb partitions for slots A and B, recovery partitions, a 64 MiB EFI system partition with L4TLauncher, a 400 MiB user data area and the APP partition, which is the ext4 root filesystem.
svg.text: Where everything lives: two storage devices, not one SD card
Sizes are read from NVIDIA's partition files: bootloader/generic/cfg/flash_t234_qspi.xml and tools/kernel_flash/flash_l4t_t234_nvme.xml.
+ UEFI variables, UEFI FTW, reserved, backup GPT, version info (≈1.4 MiB)
One boot chain (the B_ copy is identical in layout)
Two complete chains give fail-safe boot-firmware updates (NVIDIA: 'bootloader redundancy is enabled by default').
UEFI is 3.5 MiB: a custom logo or extra drivers must still fit.
Root device: SD card · NVMe SSD · USB drive
one GPT, written by the flash tool
second copy of the three above
user data area (mounted by you, or left empty)
backup partition table at the end
The kernel partitions serve the other boot modes; the flash tool fills them anyway.
Compare with an SD-card board: there, one file (sdcard.img) holds the bootloader at a fixed offset and one ext4 partition. Here the boot firmware is on the module,
so you can swap the root device, wipe it, or boot from NVMe without touching the firmware: the device only holds the OS.
